page: Vultr voc-c-32c-64gb-1000s-amd belongs to the Optimized Cloud Compute family, configured with dedicated compute resources tailored for compute-intensive demands. It is powered by an x86_64 AMD EPYC processor running at a base clock speed of 2.0 GHz, delivering 32 vCPUs derived from 16 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. Memory allocation is set at 64 GB of RAM, establishing a 1:2 memory-to-vCPU ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. Hardware features include 32 MB of shared L3 cache, AES and SHA-NI cryptographic acceleration, and AVX support, though AVX-512 and AMX extensions are absent. Local high-speed storage is bundled in the form of a 1000 GB NVMe SSD, and networking includes one complimentary public IPv4 address without discrete GPU acceleration.

Benchmark assessments demonstrate solid performance in both compute throughput and memory operations. The instance scored 3,132.38 in single-core stress-ng tests, ranking in the top tier, while multi-core stress-ng reached 99,610.25, placing it within the top 25%. PassMark evaluations reflect this capability with a CPU score of 64,051.5 and a top-decile memory score of 3,040.25. Memory bandwidth tests showed 346.3 GB/sec in large uncached reads and 164.36 GB/sec in large writes. Furthermore, Redis SET benchmarks demonstrated throughput exceeding 76.9 million operations per second, and Clang compilation tests placed in the upper quartile.

The 1:2 memory ratio provides high compute density, delivering strong qualitative cost efficiency for CPU-bound pipelines and parallel compilation where excess RAM would otherwise generate unneeded infrastructure overhead. However, workloads requiring massive in-memory datasets or deep learning models requiring AVX-512 vectorization will encounter architectural constraints. The instance is well matched for software compilation, CI/CD runners, caching layers, batch data processing, and mid-sized database management systems.

Lacking GPU acceleration, the machine adheres to a 1:2 memory-to-vCPU ratio designed for high computational density. Benchmark results show strong multi-core processing power with a PassMark CPU score of 64,051.5 and stress-ng performance placing in the upper quartile, alongside a top-tier PassMark memory score of 3,040.25. Memory bandwidth reaches 346.3 GB/sec on large read blocks, and Redis throughput surpasses 76.9 million operations per second. While unsuited for memory-intensive architectures or AVX-512 workloads, this configuration provides a balanced footprint for parallel software compilation, CI/CD pipelines, caching services, and distributed compute workloads.
